name: Four in a Row
intro: Learn Four in a Row in minutes: dropping discs, lines across, up and diagonal, and blocking, then the strategy that wins: the centre column, double threats and odd and even rows.

units.name: How Four in a Row works
units.blurb: Dropping discs, the three kinds of line, and blocking.

lessons.title: How to play Four in a Row: the rules
lessons.summary: Four in a Row in one minute: drop discs into a 7-column grid, take turns, and be first to line up four. Learn the rules by playing.
lessons.wrap: Drop, take turns, line up four. Next: all the ways a line can run.

steps.text:
Four in a Row is played on an upright grid: 7 columns and 6 rows. You have the gold discs and your opponent has ivory.

On your turn you drop one disc into a column. It falls to the lowest empty space. Gold always goes first.
Columns are numbered 1 to 7 from the left. Tap anywhere in a column to drop a disc into it.
steps.prompt: Drop a disc into the middle column, column 4.
steps.wrong: Column 4 is the middle one, with three columns on each side.
steps.done: It fell all the way to the bottom.

steps.text: Discs stack up. A disc dropped into a column lands on top of the ones already there.
steps.prompt: Column 3 has two discs. Tap the space where the next disc in column 3 will land.
steps.wrong: Discs fall to the lowest empty space: right on top of the two already there.

steps.text: The goal is to be the first to get four of your discs in a line.
steps.prompt: What happens if you get four in a row?
options: You score a point and play on
steps.explain: You win straight away. The game is over.

lessons.title: Four in a Row: across, up and diagonal wins
lessons.summary: A Four in a Row line can run across, up or diagonally. Practise all three ways to win, and learn what happens when the grid fills up.
lessons.wrap: Across, up and diagonal: always check all three. Next: stopping your opponent’s four.

steps.text: A line of four can run across a row.
steps.prompt: You have three in a row along the bottom. Finish it.

steps.text: It can run straight up a column.
steps.prompt: Win with a line going up.

steps.text: And it can run diagonally. Diagonals are the easiest lines to miss, for you and for your opponent.
steps.prompt: Finish the diagonal.
steps.wrong: Follow the marked discs up and to the right. Which column holds the next space?
steps.done: Four on the diagonal. Diagonals win a lot of games.

steps.text: Sometimes nobody manages a line before the grid is full.
steps.prompt: What happens if all 42 spaces fill up with no four in a row?
options: The player with more discs wins
steps.explain: It’s a draw. Both players have 21 discs.

lessons.title: Blocking in Four in a Row: stop the other four
lessons.summary: Before every move, check whether your opponent can win next turn. Learn to spot and block their threats across rows and diagonals.
lessons.wrap: Check for their threats before every move. Next: a quick rules check.

steps.text:
Ivory has three in a row along the bottom. If you don’t stop it, Ivory wins next turn.

A space where a player could win on their next move is called a threat.
steps.prompt: Block Ivory’s four.
steps.done: Blocked. Always look for the other player’s threats first.

steps.text: Diagonal threats are easy to miss.
steps.prompt: Ivory can win next turn. Find the space and fill it.
steps.wrong: Look at the ivory discs climbing from the bottom left. Where would the fourth one go?
steps.done: Good spot. That diagonal would have beaten you.

steps.text: One block stops one threat.
steps.prompt: Your opponent has two different spaces that would each win. What can you do?
options: Block one; they win with the other
steps.explain: You can only block one, so they win with the other. That’s why two threats at once is so strong. You’ll learn to make them yourself soon.

units.name: Rules check
units.blurb: Show you know the rules, then on to strategy.

lessons.title: Four in a Row rules check
lessons.summary: A quick Four in a Row rules check: win in a line, block a threat and answer a question. Pass it to move on to strategy.
lessons.wrap: Rules done. Now for the ideas that win games, starting with the middle column.

steps.text: Three questions. First: a chance to win.
steps.prompt: Win the game.

steps.text: Now it’s Ivory who is close.
steps.prompt: Stop Ivory from winning.

steps.text: Last one.
steps.prompt: Where does a disc go when you drop it into a column?
options: Anywhere you tap in the column
steps.explain: It falls to the lowest empty space in that column.

units.name: Winning ideas
units.blurb: The centre, double threats, traps and the endgame count.

lessons.title: Four in a Row strategy: play the centre column
lessons.summary: Why the centre column is the best place to start in Four in a Row: more winning lines run through the middle than through any edge.
lessons.wrap: Start in the middle and keep coming back to it. Next: making two threats at once.

steps.text:
Every line of four across the board has to pass through the middle column, because the grid is only 7 wide.

Discs in the middle take part in more lines than discs at the edges.
Count the lines of four that could use the bottom middle space: four across, one up and two diagonals.
steps.prompt: How many different lines of four go through the bottom middle space?
steps.explain: Seven. The bottom corner space is in just three. A middle disc works more than twice as hard.

steps.text: That’s why strong players open in the middle.
steps.prompt: Make the best first move.
steps.wrong: Go for the column that every horizontal line has to cross.
steps.done: The centre. A good habit for every game.

lessons.title: Four in a Row double threats: two ways to win
lessons.summary: The surest way to win at Four in a Row is a double threat: two winning spaces at once. Learn to set one up so a single block can’t stop it.
lessons.wrap: Two threats at once and the game is yours. Next: a trap hiding under your feet.

steps.text:
One threat can be blocked. Two threats at once can’t: your opponent only gets one disc.

You have two discs together on the bottom row, with open space on both sides.
steps.prompt: Drop a disc that makes two winning spaces at once.
steps.wrong: Make three in a row with an empty space at both ends.
steps.done: Three in a row, open at both ends. Ivory can only block one side.

steps.text: Now finish it off. Ivory will block one end.
steps.prompt: Make the double threat, then win.
steps.wrong: Same idea as before: three in a row, open at both ends.
steps.good: Two threats! Now watch Ivory block one…
steps.next: Ivory blocked one end. Win at the other.
steps.done: One block, two threats: that’s a win.

lessons.title: Four in a Row trap: don’t fill the space below
lessons.summary: In Four in a Row, the space under your opponent’s threat is poison. Learn to spot it so you never hand them the winning spot.
lessons.wrap: Before every move, check what your disc lets the other player do next. Next: odd and even rows.

steps.text: Ivory has three in a row on the third row. The fourth space is empty, but nobody can play there yet: the space under it is still empty.
steps.prompt: Tap the space Ivory needs.
steps.wrong: Follow Ivory’s three discs on the third row. Which empty space would make four?
steps.done: That space. Ivory can’t drop there until something fills the space below.

steps.text: If you drop a disc into column 5, it lands right under Ivory’s winning space, and Ivory wins on top of it.
steps.prompt: Make any move that doesn’t hand Ivory the win.
steps.wrong: Column 5 fills the space under Ivory’s threat, and Ivory drops in on top and wins. Choose another column.
steps.done: Safe. Leave that column alone for as long as you can.

lessons.title: Four in a Row endgames: odd and even rows
lessons.summary: Why threats on odd rows help the first player and even rows help the second: the counting rule behind Four in a Row endgames.
lessons.wrap: Gold wants threats on odd rows, Ivory on even rows. That’s the Four in a Row path complete!

steps.text:
Late in the game, players often have threats that neither side can reach yet, like the one in the last lesson. Then the board fills up column by column.

When the board fills evenly, the first player tends to get the spaces on odd rows: 1, 3 and 5, counting from the bottom. The second player gets even rows: 2, 4 and 6.
So a waiting threat is worth most to the right player.
steps.prompt: You moved first. Where is a waiting threat strongest for you?
steps.explain: Odd rows. When the columns fill up, those spaces tend to fall to the first player.

steps.text: And when you go second…
steps.prompt: Playing second, which rows should your waiting threats be on?
steps.explain: Even rows. A threat on row 2, 4 or 6 is one the first player usually has to give you in the end.
